newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Ally bogs down Brazil president's re-election bid.
newsitem.headline: Ally bogs down Brazil president's re-election bid.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso can no longer take for granted the support of Brazil's largest political party, a party that was a staunch ally in approving his economic reform drive, analysts said.
With 102 congressmen and 22 senators, the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) holds more Congressional seats than any other.
But last weekend it showed another a more disorderly side of itself at its convention, tossing some obstacles in Cardoso's effort to run for a second term.

The party's lack of cohesion became apparent Sunday when anti-government delegates to its convention carried the day in recommending the party vote against a constitutional amendment allowing re-election and to delay any vote on it until after February 15 -- a surprise to political observers.

The February 15 date would presumably give the PMDB leverage to make a grab for the presidencies of both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, instead of just one, by withholding their votes on re-election.
However, soon after the convention, some PMDB members appeared more conciliatory.

Earlier today, PMDB legislators seemed to ignore those positions and voted in a Congressional panel to allow a constitutional amendment on re-election -- setting aside the spirit of the convention's resolutions.

But also today some PMDB party leaders reconfirmed they would not vote on the re-election amendment in the Lower House until after February 15. The vote on the floor of the lower house, where Cardoso needs a three-fifths majority, will be the real test for the amendment.
"The bottom line is that the outlook for re-election is looking a whole lot harder," said analyst Bolivar Lamounier.

The lack of a unifying party ideology makes PMDB support a wild card, observers say. Though Cardoso may eventually sway the PMDB's votes in the Chamber of Deputies and Senate, he will have to do a good deal of horse-trading and possibly change his re-election strategy to keep the proposal afloat.

A ragtag band of nationalists, former communists and a handful of political barons from Brazil's feudal hinterland, the PMDB is the successor of the Brazilian Democratic Movement, which in the 60's and 70's bitterly opposed Brazil's 21-year military dictatorship.
But it has been incapable of evolving beyond old-style Brazilian politics and its nationalist anti-military platform. Today its biggest asset is the number of legislators it can assemble in Congress.
"This party doesn't exist. It represents a bunch of feudal groups each doing their own thing," said a congressional PMDB official who asked not to be named.

Nonetheless, Cardoso is not without resources. In a meeting with PMDB leaders Monday, Cardoso urged the party to meet its commitments and warned that if the amendment did not pass he would expel the PMDB from the ruling coalition.
That could be a very high price to pay since besides holding four cabinet-level seats, the PMDB controls over 100 high-paying posts in the administration.
But more importantly is the threat of a plebiscite, which would bypass politicians altogether and take the issue to the people, who would likely give Cardoso a victory.
But neither side is eager for a drawn-out plebiscite.
"In the end, (the amendment) is going to be approved by Congress, because a referendum would be bad for everyone, but it's going to be very difficult," said Robert Drummond of Bozano, Simonsen.
